title: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What
summary: Lesson 1.04 introduced the four build stages. This lesson goes deeper into the rules that decide which file needs what: **declarations** versus **definitions**, headers and include guards, the **one definition rule**, `inline` and `static`, and how the linker matches **symbols** between object files. These rules explain almost every "already defined" and "unresolved" error you will meet.
markdown:
## Declarations and definitions C++ separates saying something exists from saying what it is. | | Declaration: "this exists" | Definition: "here it is" | |---|---|---| | Function | `int addBonus(int score);` | `int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; }` | | Global variable | `extern int g_highScore;` | `int g_highScore{ 0 };` | | Class | `class Player;` (a forward declaration) | `class Player { int health; };` | A declaration is enough to **use** a function: the compiler only needs to know its name, parameters and return type to generate a call. The call's target address is left for the linker. A definition is what produces machine code or storage. ## Headers carry declarations Each `.cpp` file is compiled alone (it becomes one **translation unit**). For `main.cpp` to call a function defined in `score.cpp`, `main.cpp` needs its declaration. A header file is simply a convenient way to paste the same declarations into every file that needs them: ```cpp // score.h #pragma once int addBonus(int score); // declaration // score.cpp #include "score.h" int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; } // the one definition // main.cpp #include "score.h" int main() { return addBonus(10); } // a call, resolved by the linker ``` `#pragma once` stops a header from being pasted twice into the same translation unit, which would otherwise repeat its class definitions and fail. The older, portable form is an **include guard**: ```cpp #ifndef SCORE_H #define SCORE_H int addBonus(int score); #endif ``` ## The one definition rule The **one definition rule** (ODR) says, roughly: - every function and global variable that is used must be **defined exactly once** in the whole program; - a class, an `inline` function or a template may be defined in **every** translation unit that uses it, but all those definitions must be identical. That second point is why class definitions and templates live in headers, and why ordinary function bodies do not. Break the first point and the linker complains: | Situation | Linker error | |---|---| | A function is declared and called, but defined nowhere | `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol` | | A function body written in a header included by two `.cpp` files | `LNK2005: already defined in main.obj` | | A global `int g_score{ 0 };` in a header | `LNK2005` as well | ## Ways to make a definition safe in a header | Keyword | Effect | Use for | |---|---|---| | `inline` | "Identical definitions may appear in many files; keep one" | Small functions in headers; `inline` variables (C++17) for header constants | | `static` (at namespace scope) | "Private to this translation unit": each file gets its own separate copy | Helpers used only in one `.cpp` | | Unnamed `namespace { ... }` | Same as `static`, for everything inside | Several file-private helpers | | `constexpr` variable | Implicitly `inline` (since C++17) for static data members; namespace-scope `constexpr` variables are internal to each file | Compile-time constants | Templates and functions defined inside a class body are implicitly `inline`, which is why they can live in headers. ## Symbols: what the linker actually matches Each object file contains a **symbol table**: names it defines and names it needs. C++ names are **mangled** into strings that encode the namespace, parameter types and more, so that overloads get different symbols: ``` int addBonus(int) ?addBonus@@YAHH@Z int addBonus(float) ?addBonus@@YAHM@Z void Player::heal(int) ?heal@Player@@QEAAXH@Z ``` The linker matches these strings exactly. So a declaration that differs from its definition in any detail (a `const`, a parameter type, a namespace) produces a *different* symbol, and the result is `LNK2019` even though "the function is right there". The error message shows the mangled name and a readable version; compare it carefully with your definition. `extern "C"` turns mangling off, giving the plain name `addBonus`. That is how C++ code exposes functions to C, and how DLLs usually export functions so other languages and `GetProcAddress` (lesson 4.05) can find them by a simple name. You can see an object file's symbols with: ```powershell dumpbin /symbols score.obj dumpbin /exports plugin.dll undname "?addBonus@@YAHH@Z" ``` ## Order of the stages, once more ```mermaid flowchart LR A["a.cpp"] --> PA["preprocess"] --> CA["compile"] --> OA["a.obj
defines: addBonus
needs: printf"] B["main.cpp"] --> PB["preprocess"] --> CB["compile"] --> OB["main.obj
defines: main
needs: addBonus"] OA --> L["link"] OB --> L LIB["libraries"] --> L L --> E["game.exe"] ``` Changing `a.cpp` recompiles only `a.obj`, then re-links. Changing a header recompiles every `.cpp` that includes it, directly or indirectly. That is why large projects keep headers small, use forward declarations where they can, and avoid including heavy headers in other headers. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] A declaration that does not quite match its definition > `void heal(int)` declared, `void heal(long)` defined: two different symbols, and an unresolved external. Copy declarations from definitions exactly. > [!warning] Globals defined in headers > Declare `extern int g_score;` in the header and define it in one `.cpp`, or use `inline int g_score{ 0 };`. > [!warning] Including a header to get a type you only point to > If a header only uses `Player*` or `Player&`, a forward declaration `class Player;` is enough, and saves recompiling when `player.h` changes. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does the one definition rule require? - Every function may be declared only once in the program - Each `.cpp` file may define only one function + Each used function and variable is defined exactly once in the program - Every header may be included only once in the whole program > Declarations may be repeated freely. It is definitions of ordinary functions and variables that must be unique. Classes, templates and inline functions may be defined in several files, but only if every definition is identical. ? Why do class definitions go in headers but function bodies usually do not? - Function bodies are too long for headers - Headers can only contain types, not code - The compiler reads headers before `.cpp` files, so bodies there would run first + Classes may be defined (identically) in every translation unit; ordinary functions must be defined only once > A function body in a header included by two `.cpp` files is defined twice, which breaks the one definition rule unless it is marked `inline`. ? What is name mangling? - Shortening long names to save space in the `.exe` + Encoding a function's namespace, class and parameter types into its symbol - Hiding names so the program cannot be reverse engineered - Renaming variables that clash with keywords > That is how overloads such as `heal(int)` and `heal(unsigned)` get distinct symbols, and why they do not link to each other. ? Which is a definition, not just a declaration? - `int addBonus(int score);` - `extern int g_lives;` + `int g_lives{ 3 };` > It creates the variable's storage. The others only announce that something exists elsewhere. ? Two `.cpp` files include a header containing `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`. What happens? - It compiles and links fine + The linker reports that `square` is already defined - The compiler reports a syntax error > Each file gets a definition, breaking the one definition rule. Marking it `inline` fixes it. ? Why does a declaration `void heal(int)` not link to a definition `void heal(unsigned)`? - The linker ignores parameters - `unsigned` cannot be used in definitions + Parameter types are part of the mangled symbol name > C++ symbols encode the parameter types so that overloads can coexist. ? What does `extern "C"` change? + It turns off name mangling, so the symbol is the plain name - It makes the function run faster - It makes the function private to one file > Plain names are what C code, other languages and `GetProcAddress` expect. ```
ideas:
- Put a function body in a header included by two `.cpp` files and read the `LNK2005` error. Fix it with `inline`, then instead by moving the body to a `.cpp`.
- Run `dumpbin /symbols` on an object file and find your functions' mangled names. Feed one to `undname`.
- Change a parameter type in a definition but not in its declaration, and read the `LNK2019` message's mangled name.

cards.q: What does the one definition rule require?
cards.a:
Each used function and variable is defined exactly once in the program

Declarations may be repeated freely. It is definitions of ordinary functions and variables that must be unique. Classes, templates and inline functions may be defined in several files, but only if every definition is identical.

cards.q: Why do class definitions go in headers but function bodies usually do not?
cards.a:
Classes may be defined (identically) in every translation unit; ordinary functions must be defined only once

A function body in a header included by two `.cpp` files is defined twice, which breaks the one definition rule unless it is marked `inline`.

Encoding a function's namespace, class and parameter types into its symbol

That is how overloads such as `heal(int)` and `heal(unsigned)` get distinct symbols, and why they do not link to each other.

cards.q: Which is a definition, not just a declaration?
cards.a:
`int g_lives{ 3 };`

It creates the variable's storage. The others only announce that something exists elsewhere.

cards.q: Two `.cpp` files include a header containing `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`. What happens?
cards.a:
The linker reports that `square` is already defined

Each file gets a definition, breaking the one definition rule. Marking it `inline` fixes it.

cards.q: Why does a declaration `void heal(int)` not link to a definition `void heal(unsigned)`?
cards.a:
Parameter types are part of the mangled symbol name

C++ symbols encode the parameter types so that overloads can coexist.

It turns off name mangling, so the symbol is the plain name

Plain names are what C code, other languages and `GetProcAddress` expect.
